q: Human eye consists of sense organs which are capable of receiving visual images and sending the information to the brain.
e: True. The brain interprets that picture as upright. The eye receives visual images and sends them to the brain along the optic nerve. The retinal image is real, inverted and smaller than the object.

q: The front portion of the eye is covered by a tough, opaque membrane called the cornea.
e: False. The cornea is a tough transparent membrane at the front of the eye. Opaque would block the image before it started. Light has to enter there.

q: The region between the cornea and the eyelens is filled with a transparent liquid called the aqueous humour.
e: True. Aqueous humour is the transparent liquid between cornea and eyelens. Vitreous humour fills the larger chamber between eyelens and retina. Those two jellies are not interchangeable.

q: The region between the eyelens and the retina contains a transparent liquid called the aqueous humour.
e: False. Between eyelens and retina sits vitreous humour. Aqueous humour fills the front chamber between cornea and lens. Swap those names and you have put the jelly in the wrong room.

q: The iris which is the colored portion of the eye controls the amount of light energy entering the eye.
e: True. The pupil dilates in dim light and contracts in bright light. The iris is the coloured part of the eye and controls how much light enters. The pupil is the hole in its centre, the eye's aperture.

q: The pupil is in the centre of the iris and the light passes through it.
e: True. The pupil dilates in dim light and contracts in bright light. The iris is the coloured part of the eye and controls how much light enters. Pupil is in the centre of the cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: The pupil automatically contracts in dim light and dilates in bright light.
e: False. The pupil dilates in dim light and contracts in bright light. That is the iris working as the camera aperture. The wrong way round would dazzle you in sun and starve you in shade.

q: The ciliary muscles are attached to the eyelens.
e: True. Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex. For distant objects they relax and the lens flattens.

q: The ciliary muscles can vary the thickness of the eyelens, thus alter the focal length of the lens to obtain a sharp image on the retina.
e: True. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex. For distant objects they relax and the lens flattens. Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length.

q: When near objects are viewed, the ciliary muscles relax and permit the eyelens to form a less convex shape.
e: False. For a near object the ciliary muscles contract and the eyelens becomes more convex. Relaxation and a flatter lens are for distant objects. Accommodation is that thickness change.

q: When distant objects are viewed, the ciliary muscles relax and the eyelens becomes less convex.
e: True. For distant objects they relax and the lens flattens. Ciliary muscles attach to the eyelens and change its thickness, hence its focal length. For near objects they contract and the lens becomes more convex.

q: The retina is the light sensitive area of the cells, at the back of the eye.
e: True. The image there is real, inverted and smaller than the object. The optic nerve then carries that signal to the brain. The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, with rods and cones.

q: The retina consists of rods and cones.
e: True. The yellow spot is cone-packed and most sensitive for fine detail. The blind spot has no rods or cones, where the optic nerve leaves. The retina at the back of the eye holds rods and cones.

q: The yellow spot which is the least light-sensitive spot on the retina is used for viewing very small objects.
e: False. The yellow spot is the most light-sensitive region and is packed with cones. The blind spot is the insensitive patch with no rods or cones. Fine detail is a yellow-spot job.

q: The yellow spot consists of cones exclusively.
e: True. yellow and spot have to stay with the same process. A different driver in place of yellow would describe a different law.

q: There is a spot on the retina which has no rods or cones called the blind spot.
e: True. The blind spot has no rods or cones, where the optic nerve leaves. The retina at the back of the eye holds rods and cones. The yellow spot is cone-packed and most sensitive for fine detail.

q: The light energy falling on the retina is transmitted to the brain by the ciliary nerve.
e: False. The optic nerve carries the retinal signal to the brain. Ciliary muscles only squeeze the lens. Nerve and muscle are different jobs.

q: The cornea, the aqueous humour, the eyelens and the vitreous humour are refracting substances.
e: True. Opaque would block the image at the door. Aqueous humour then fills the chamber behind it, before the eyelens. Aqueous humour is the transparent liquid between cornea and eyelens.

q: The image of an object formed on the retina by these four substances is virtual, erect and smaller than the size of the object.
e: False. The retinal image is real, inverted, and smaller than the object. The brain reads that inverted picture as upright. Virtual erect images belong to simple magnifiers, not to the retina.

q: Farsightedness is a defect of vision in which distant objects are seen clearly, but objects nearby are blurry.
e: True. Farsightedness, hyperopia: distant objects are clear, nearby ones are blurry. Near rays meet behind the retina, so a converging convex lens is the correction. A diverging lens is the myopia tool, not this one.

q: Nearsightedness is a defect of vision in which near objects are seen clearly, but objects far away are blurry.
e: True. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Nearsightedness, myopia: near objects are clear, distant ones are blurry.

q: For a person with farsightedness, the rays from near objects intersect at a point in front of the retina after passing through the eyelens.
e: False. In farsightedness, near rays meet behind the retina. In front of the retina is the myopia meeting point for distant rays. Convex spectacles add the extra convergence hyperopia needs.

q: Farsightedness is due to an eyeball which is too short or due to the eyelens which cannot be sufficiently convex.
e: True. Farsightedness, hyperopia: distant objects are clear, nearby ones are blurry. Near rays meet behind the retina, so a converging convex lens is the correction. Farsightedness is due to an eyeball which cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Farsightedness can be corrected by the use of spectacles with diverging lens or concave lens.
e: False. Farsightedness needs a converging convex lens. A diverging concave lens is the myopia correction. Hyperopia is not enough bending; you add a convex lens, you do not take bending away.

q: For a person with nearsightedness, the rays from distant objects intersect at a point in front of the retina after passing through the eyelens.
e: True. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Person with nearsightedness the rays from distant cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Nearsightedness is due to an eyeball which is too long or due to the eyelens which is more convex than is necessary.
e: True. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens is the correction. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Nearsightedness is due to an eyeball which cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Nearsightedness can be corrected by the use of spectacles with converging lens or convex lens.
e: False. Nearsightedness needs a diverging concave lens so distant rays meet on the retina, not in front of it. A convex lens would add even more convergence. Myopia and hyperopia take opposite spectacles.

q: For normal vision the least distance of distinct vision is about $25	ext{ cm}$.
e: True. The far point for normal vision is infinity. Least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm for a normal eye. Nearer than that, the lens cannot bulge enough.

q: For normal vision the maximum distance of distinct vision is infinity.
e: True. Half-integer path difference is a minimum. A bright maximum needs constructive interference, integer path difference. On a grating, d sin theta = m lambda locates those maxima.
